notes.claim: The first law defines the change in a system's internal energy as the heat transferred into it minus the work it does.
It is impossible to convert all heat from a reservoir into work in a cyclical process that returns the system to its original state.
In a reciprocating engine, the exhaust gas and cooling systems generally carry 60 to 70 percent of the inlet fuel energy.
For large marine two-stroke engines, about half of the fuel energy is lost as waste heat (a 2025 marine paper).
A diesel is a compression ignition engine; it can run a higher compression ratio than a petrol (Otto) engine because only air is compressed, so the fuel cannot ignite early (for i4's diesel outline).
Seawater's specific heat is about 3,850 J per kg per °C (for i4's cooler sum).

sources.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
sources.quote: The first law of thermodynamics defines the internal energy (E) as equal to the difference of the heat transfer (Q) into a system and the work (W) done by the system.
